---
title: "Using pkiaas from an AI Agent"
description: "How AI agents run the pkiaas CLI: JSON output, passphrases and other secrets, logging in, and what to do about each error code."
---
<!-- Generated by `pkiaas docs` from the CLI's commands (cli/internal/cli in the pkiaas repository); don't edit by hand. -->

`pkiaas` manages PKIaaS certificate authorities and makes keys, certificate signing requests (CSRs) and PKCS#12
files on the user's computer. It is built to be run by AI agents as well as people. This guide is for agents.

## Rules

- **Add `--json` to every command.** Standard output then holds exactly one JSON value: the result, or
  `{"error": {"code", "message", "hint"}}`. Messages for people (progress, notices, update hints) go to standard
  error; don't parse them. Use the exit code and the error `code`, not the message text.
- **Look commands up rather than guess.** `pkiaas help --json` describes every command: its flags, examples, result
  fields, side effects, and whether it calls the server, needs a login or needs the user, with the exit codes and
  error codes. `pkiaas help --json key create` (or `pkiaas key create --help --json`) describes one command.
- **pkiaas never prompts without a terminal.** When something is missing, such as a passphrase, it fails with the
  `usage` code and names the flag to give. Don't pipe answers to prompts. Only `pkiaas login` waits, for the user to
  approve the login.
- **Files are never overwritten** unless `--force` is given (error `file_exists`). Only add `--force` when the user
  wants the file replaced. If you ran the command before and lost its output, the file it wrote is the result: use
  it rather than making another key.
- **Private keys stay on this computer.** Pass key files by path. Don't read, print or copy their contents, and
  don't send them anywhere.

## Secrets

Your commands and their output may be logged, so keep secrets out of both.

- Passphrases are never command-line arguments. Give them with `--passphrase-env NAME` (an environment variable
  the user has set) or `--passphrase-file PATH` (the first line of a file). Commands that read a key and write
  another file take `--key-passphrase-env` and `--key-passphrase-file` for the key's passphrase.
- Ask the user to set the variable or write the file themselves. Don't put a passphrase in a command you run, for
  example `echo secret | pkiaas ...` or `export KEY_PASSPHRASE=secret`.
- If you have to make a passphrase up, generate it into a file without printing it, and tell the user where it is,
  so they can move it to a password manager: `(umask 077; openssl rand -base64 32 > server.key.pass)`, or without
  OpenSSL `(umask 077; head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 > server.key.pass)`. In PowerShell:
  `[Convert]::ToBase64String([Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::GetBytes(32)) | Set-Content server.key.pass`.
- Keys are encrypted by default. Only use `--no-passphrase` when the user asks for an unencrypted key, e.g. for a
  service that loads its key at startup without a passphrase.
- pkiaas never prints keys, passphrases or tokens. Don't print `PKIAAS_TOKEN`, and don't read the CLI's
  `hosts.json`.

## Logging in

Commands that call the server need a login. Run `pkiaas whoami --json` to check one: exit code 3 with
`not_logged_in` or `invalid_token` means there is none.

Logging in needs the user, who approves it in their browser.

- Ask the user to run `pkiaas login` themselves. In Claude Code, they can type `! pkiaas login`.
- Where no browser can open on this computer (SSH, containers), they run `pkiaas login --device`. It prints an
  address and a code to enter in a browser on any device.
- If the user can't run commands, you can run `pkiaas login --device --json` yourself. Start it in the background
  (it waits up to 10 minutes for the user's approval), read the address and code from its standard error as soon
  as they appear, and pass them to the user. Keep it running until it exits; its standard output is then the
  result. Never enter a code in a browser yourself, and never approve a login you didn't start for the user.
- In CI, set `PKIAAS_TOKEN` from the CI system's secret store instead of logging in.

The login is kept for 30 days of inactivity, and for at most 90 days. `pkiaas logout` revokes it.

## Certificate authorities

`pkiaas ca list --json` lists the user's CAs: their own and those they were invited to. Each has an `id` and a
`name`, and `signed` (false while the CA waits for its certificate).

Commands take a CA by its name, in any case (e.g. `--ca "Example Issuing CA"`), or by its `id`. Use names with
people: say the CA's name to the user, and accept the name they give. Use IDs in scripts and in commands you keep:
an ID never changes, while a CA can be renamed and two CAs can share a name. A name that more than one of the
user's CAs has fails with `ca_ambiguous`, whose message lists their IDs: ask the user which one they mean.

One CA is active: commands that work in a CA use it unless told otherwise. `pkiaas ca show --json` says which one
it is and why. Login makes it the CA the user last worked in on the website; `pkiaas ca set NAME --json` (or
`ID`) changes it, and keeps the ID, so renaming the CA doesn't change it. The active CA is kept on this computer
for that server; setting it doesn't change the CA the user works in on the website. Before working in a CA, check
that the active one is the CA the user means; when they have more than one and haven't said which, ask them
rather than choosing.

To work in another CA without changing the active one, give `--ca NAME` (or `ID`) to the command, or set
`PKIAAS_CA` to its name or ID in its environment. `--ca` comes first, then `PKIAAS_CA`, then the active CA;
`source` in `pkiaas ca show --json` says which chose it (`flag`, `environment`, or `set`, `website`, `first` for
the active CA). A name or ID the account doesn't have fails with `not_found`.

`pkiaas ca show --json` also gives the CA's details: `signed`, its key (`keyType`, `keySize`, `hsm`), its
certificate (`serial`, `thumbprint`, `validFrom`, `validTo`), `activeCertificates`, and `urls` with its public
services: certificate, chain, CRL, OCSP, time stamping, the CPS page and Windows enrollment (CEP/CES).

`pkiaas ca export --out FILE --json` saves the CA's certificate; with `--chain`, the CA's certificate followed by
those that issued it. The chain is what `pkiaas pkcs12 create --chain-file` and servers (e.g. nginx after the server's
certificate) need; a root CA's certificate is what clients add to their trust store. A CA that isn't signed yet
fails with `ca_not_signed`. (`ca cert`, its name in 0.1.0, still works but is deprecated.)

## Exporting

`ca export` and `cert export` work the same way, as `openssl x509` does:

- Without `--out`, the output goes to standard output, ready to pipe into another command; there is no result
  then, so `--json` needs `--out FILE`. With `--out FILE --json`, the file is written and the result describes it.
- `--format pem` (default) or `--format der`, as OpenSSL's `-outform`. PEM is what servers, OpenSSL and
  `pkcs12 create` read; DER is the binary form (`.cer`, `.der`) Windows and Java also take. DER holds one
  certificate, so it can't be combined with `--chain`. Redirect or pipe DER: it is binary.
- `--chain` adds the certificates that issued it, up to the root. `--force` replaces an existing `--out` file.

Prefer `--out FILE --json`: you get the file and a result to check (`content`, `certificates`, `format`). Use
standard output only to pipe the output straight into another command.

## Standard input and output

The local commands work the same way: `key create`, `csr create` and `pkcs12 create` write to standard output
without `--out` (then `--json` needs `--out FILE`), and `key create` and `csr create` take `--format pem|der`
(`pkcs12 create` always writes DER). Their input files, `--key`, `--cert` and `--chain-file`, may be `-` for
standard input; PEM or DER is recognized from the content. Only one input or passphrase per command can come
from standard input, and with data on standard input passphrases can't be prompted for, so give them with
`--*passphrase-env` or `--*passphrase-file FILE`.

Keys and PKCS#12 files are secrets: always write them with `--out FILE` (owner-only), never to standard output,
since your transcript is kept. Pipe certificates and CSRs instead, e.g.
`pkiaas cert export SERIAL --chain | pkiaas pkcs12 create --cert - --key server.key ... --out server.pfx`.

In Windows PowerShell 5.1, `>` and `|` re-encode output, which breaks keys, certificates and PKCS#12 files: always
use `--out FILE` there, and give file names rather than `-`. PowerShell 7.4 and later keep the bytes. A file
re-encoded this way fails with a message saying so.

## Certificates

`pkiaas cert list --json` lists the certificates the CA issued, newest first: also expired and revoked ones, and
the CAs it signed. Each has a `serial`, which the other `cert` commands take to name it in its CA, a `status`
(`valid`, `expired` or `revoked`) and `revocation` (reason and date, or null). It returns the first `--limit`
(default 50, at most 1000); `total` says how many match, so when it is larger, narrow the list rather than reading
everything: `--search TEXT` keeps certificates whose common name contains the text, and `--sort FIELD` (name,
revocationReason, template, validFrom, validTo, keyType or keySize) with `--order asc|desc` brings the ones you
need first. Like every command that works in a CA, they take `--ca NAME` (or `ID`), and their results name the CA
in `issuer` (`id` and `name`).

- `pkiaas cert show SERIAL --json` gives a certificate's details; with `--text`, `text` holds every field and
  extension as `openssl x509 -text` prints them (e.g. its subject alternative names). Serials are hex, with or
  without colons, in any case. A serial the CA didn't issue fails with `not_found`.
- `pkiaas cert export SERIAL --out FILE --json` saves the certificate (see "Exporting" above); with `--chain`,
  followed by the CA's certificate and its issuers, which is what a server sends (e.g. nginx's `ssl_certificate`).
- `pkiaas cert export SERIAL --csr --out FILE --json` saves the CSR it was issued from, when `hasCsr` is true
  (otherwise `csr_not_stored`). A CSR sent by SCEP holds the enrollment's challenge password: the file is
  owner-only; don't print it or put it in your output.

To find the certificate for a name, e.g. before renewing it: `pkiaas cert list --search www.example.com --json`,
and take the newest one whose `status` is `valid`.

### Revoking

Revoking stops a certificate from being trusted: the CA's next CRL and OCSP responses list it. Clients that check
revocation stop accepting it, so **ask the user before revoking**, naming the certificate (name and serial) and the
reason, and only then run the command with `--yes`. Without `--yes` and without a terminal, it fails with `usage`.

- `pkiaas cert revoke SERIAL --reason REASON --yes --json`. The reasons are RFC 5280's: `unspecified`,
  `keyCompromise` (its private key leaked or may have), `cACompromise`, `affiliationChanged`, `superseded` (replaced
  by a new certificate), `cessationOfOperation` (no longer used) and `certificateHold` (suspended for now).
- Only `certificateHold` can be undone: `pkiaas cert unrevoke SERIAL --json` takes the certificate off hold. A
  certificate on hold can also be revoked for good with another reason. Every other reason is final; changing or
  undoing it fails with `revocation_final`.
- Both are safe to run again: revoking with the same reason, or unrevoking a certificate that isn't revoked,
  changes nothing and succeeds.
- Both need a subscription, the user's or the CA owner's; without one they fail with
  `subscription_required`. Tell the user rather than retrying.

Requests that are safe to repeat (reading, revoking, unrevoking, and requesting a certificate with its Idempotency-Key) are tried up to 3
times in all when the connection fails or the server answers with a 5xx or 429; a notice goes to standard error. Only run a command again yourself after it has
failed. When the server asks to wait longer than 10 seconds, the command fails at once and its message says how long
to wait before running it again.

## Requesting certificates

`pkiaas request create --csr FILE --template NAME --json` sends a CSR (PEM or DER, `-` for standard input) to the CA.
The request waits for a member of the CA to approve it, which issues the certificate. No email is sent. Add
`--approve` to approve it in the same command when the user wants the certificate issued now: the result is then
`issued`, with the certificate's `serial`, and `--out FILE` (or `--out -`) writes the certificate too. Otherwise tell the user the request's `id` and that it waits for
approval.

- `--template` is the name of a template from `pkiaas template list --json` whose `enabled` is true, in any case
  (e.g. `--template "Web Server"`), or its `id`. A template says what the certificate holds (validity, key usages
  and so on); if more than one fits, ask the user which to use. A wrong or disabled one fails with
  `template_not_found`; a name that two enabled templates share fails with `template_ambiguous`: use the `id`.
- The server checks the CSR's signature; an unreadable or altered CSR fails with `invalid_csr`. Only the CSR is
  sent, never anything else in the file.

**Keep the idempotency key.** Each run is a new request. To make a create safe to repeat, make a key for it (e.g.
a UUID), pass it with `--idempotency-key KEY`, and keep it with your notes. If you can't tell whether the command
worked (it timed out, or a later session picks up the work), run it again with the same CSR, template, CA and key:
within 24 hours that returns the first result rather than a second request. Without the flag, the CLI makes a key
and reports it as `idempotencyKey`. A key used for a different request fails with `idempotency_key_reused`, and
one whose first request hasn't finished with `idempotency_key_in_use` (wait, then retry with the same key). After 24
hours the key is forgotten and the command makes a new request. With `--approve`, the same command and key
approves the same request, which is safe: an issued request stays as it is. If the approval fails, the request
stays (waiting for approval) and the error says its `id`.

### Pending requests

`pkiaas request list --json` lists the CA's requests that wait for something, as the website's Pending Requests
page does; `pkiaas request show ID --json` shows one with what its CSR asks for (`subject`, `subjectAltNames`,
`keyType`). `status` says what each waits for:

- `pendingApproval`: a member of the CA approves or declines it. With `hasCsr` true, `pkiaas request approve ID`
  issues it; one without a CSR needs an approved voucher, which only the website sends.
- `pendingEmailVerification`: the requester has yet to confirm their email address.
- `preApproved`: it is issued when the requester picks it up with its voucher or SCEP challenge.
- `processing`: it is being signed, which takes seconds. One processing for more than 10 minutes
  (`processingSince`) is stuck: it can be declined, and the requester makes a new request.

Approving and declining are the user's decisions: approve or decline only the requests the user asked you to, and
check each with `pkiaas request show` first. Approving issues a certificate for whatever the request's template
allows; declining is final.

- `pkiaas request approve ID --json` ends once the certificate is issued and gives its `serial`; with `--out FILE`
  (and `--chain`) it writes the certificate too. It is safe to run
  again: an issued request stays as it is. It fails with `request_not_approvable` (no CSR, email not confirmed,
  pre-approved, or changes to a request that isn't `readyToBeSigned`), `request_declined`, `request_processing` (wait a few seconds and check it with `request show`), or
  `signing_failed` when the CA couldn't sign (e.g. its IoT HSM didn't answer): tell the user, whose CA log on the
  website says why. Approvals are never retried by themselves.
- **Changing what is issued.** By default the certificate holds what the CSR asks for, as the template allows.
  When the user asks for something else, `request approve` (and `request create --approve`) take `--subject DN`
  (in place of the CSR's subject; the template's subject attributes still win), `--san NAME` (repeatable; all of
  the certificate's SANs, in place of the CSR's) and `--not-after TIME` with an optional `--not-before TIME`
  (RFC 3339, e.g. `2027-01-31T00:00:00Z`; from now without `--not-before`), as the website's override boxes do.
  Only a request whose `statusDetail` is `readyToBeSigned` can be changed (otherwise `request_not_approvable`).
  Without a subscription, while `validityLimitDays` is set in `request show`, the validity can't be changed
  (`subscription_required`); values OpenSSL won't take fail with `invalid_overrides`, and nothing is signed. An
  issued request is never signed again: running the command again with other changes succeeds but applies none.
- `pkiaas request decline ID --yes --json` declines it for good. Declining a declined request succeeds; an issued
  one fails with `request_issued` (revoke its certificate instead, if the user wants that).

## Recipes

Choose a key type with `pkiaas key types --json`. The default, `rsa-2048`, works everywhere. Use `ec-p256` for
smaller, faster keys. Use `ml-dsa-*` or `slh-dsa-*` (post-quantum) only when the user asks for them, because few
clients accept them yet.

Create a key and a CSR for a TLS server (the user has set `KEY_PASSPHRASE`):

```sh
pkiaas key create --type ec-p256 --out server.key --passphrase-env KEY_PASSPHRASE --json
pkiaas csr create --key server.key --key-passphrase-env KEY_PASSPHRASE --cn www.example.com \
  --san www.example.com --san example.com --out server.csr --json
```

List the common name among the SANs too: with `--san`, it isn't added for you, and most clients only check SANs.

Then request the certificate from the user's CA, with a key you keep (see "Requesting certificates"):

```sh
pkiaas template list --json
pkiaas request create --csr server.csr --template "Web Server" --idempotency-key KEY --json
```

If the user wants it issued now, add `--approve` and `--out`: the command issues the certificate and writes it,
so no serial has to be copied between commands:

```sh
pkiaas request create --csr server.csr --template "Web Server" --approve --chain --out server.pem \
  --idempotency-key KEY --json
```

`--chain` adds the CA's certificates (what a server sends); `--out -` writes the certificate to standard output
instead, for piping, with no result. Without `--approve`, the user approves it (`pkiaas request approve ID --out
server.pem`, or the website's Pending Requests page); `pkiaas request show ID --json` gives the certificate's
`serial` for `pkiaas cert export` later.

Combine the key, the signed certificate and the CA chain into a PKCS#12 file for Windows, Java or a load balancer
(the user has set `PFX_PASSPHRASE` too):

```sh
pkiaas ca export --chain --out ca.pem --json
pkiaas pkcs12 create --key server.key --key-passphrase-env KEY_PASSPHRASE --cert server.pem --chain-file ca.pem \
  --out server.pfx --passphrase-env PFX_PASSPHRASE --json
```

Or, with the certificate's serial, without saving the certificate and chain first:

```sh
pkiaas cert export SERIAL --chain | pkiaas pkcs12 create --key server.key --key-passphrase-env KEY_PASSPHRASE \
  --cert - --out server.pfx --passphrase-env PFX_PASSPHRASE --json
```

Add `--legacy` only for systems older than Windows 10 1709, Java 12 or OpenSSL 1.1.1.

## Versions

`pkiaas version --json` shows the installed version. When the server has a newer one, pkiaas prints an update
command on standard error. If a command fails with `cli_outdated`, run the install command in the message, then run
the command again.

## Exit codes

| Exit | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ok | the command succeeded |
| 1 | error | the command failed; the error code says why |
| 2 | usage | the command line is wrong: an unknown command or flag, or missing or conflicting options |
| 3 | auth | not logged in, the login expired, or not allowed |
| 4 | not_found | the CA, certificate or other object doesn't exist |
| 5 | conflict | the operation would overwrite or clash with something that exists, e.g. an output file |

## Error codes

With `--json`, an error is `{"error": {"code", "message", "hint"}}`. The hint is what to do; when an error has none of its own, it is the one below.

| Code | Exit | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `error` | 1 | an error without a more specific code; the message says what failed | read the message: fix the cause if it is clear (e.g. a wrong file path), otherwise tell the user |
| `usage` | 2 | the command line is wrong, or a needed option (such as a passphrase without a terminal to prompt on) is missing | fix the command line; run the command with `--help` (or `pkiaas help --json <command>`) for its flags |
| `file_exists` | 5 | an output file exists, and files are never replaced without `--force` | if an earlier run of yours wrote the file, it is the result: use it; otherwise choose another output file, or add `--force` if the user wants the file replaced |
| `wrong_passphrase` | 1 | the key's passphrase is wrong, or the key file is damaged | ask the user for the right passphrase, given the same way (environment variable or file) |
| `not_logged_in` | 3 | there is no login for the server, and `PKIAAS_TOKEN` isn't set | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` (or `pkiaas login --device` where no browser can open); see `pkiaas help agents` |
| `invalid_token` | 3 | the server refused the token: the login expired, was revoked, or the account was removed | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` (or `pkiaas login --device` where no browser can open); see `pkiaas help agents` |
| `forbidden` | 3 | the account isn't allowed to do this | ask the user to check their access, or the CA owner to delegate it |
| `not_found` | 4 | the server has no such object, or the account can't see it | check the name or ID |
| `conflict` | 5 | the server refused a change that clashes with something that exists | read the message; check what exists before changing it, and ask the user before replacing anything |
| `ca_not_signed` | 5 | the CA has no certificate yet: it waits for its signed certificate to be imported | ask the user to import the CA's signed certificate on the website (the CA's page), or use another CA from `pkiaas ca list --json` (signed is true) |
| `csr_not_stored` | 4 | no CSR is stored for the certificate (e.g. one issued by ACME) | the certificate itself is still available with `pkiaas cert export SERIAL`; check `hasCsr` in `pkiaas cert show --json` before asking for a CSR |
| `subscription_required` | 3 | the feature needs a subscription, the user's or the CA owner's (revoking and unrevoking certificates; changing the validity when approving a request) | tell the user; they can subscribe, or link a subscription they already have, on the website's profile page |
| `revocation_final` | 5 | the certificate is revoked with a reason other than certificateHold, which can't be undone or changed | nothing to do: the certificate stays revoked; `pkiaas cert show SERIAL --json` shows its reason |
| `invalid_csr` | 1 | the server can't read the CSR, or its signature doesn't match its key | check that the file is the CSR (PEM or DER) and wasn't changed after it was signed; make a new one with `pkiaas csr create` |
| `template_not_found` | 4 | the CA has no enabled template with this name or ID | run `pkiaas template list --json` (with the same `--ca`) and use the name or id of a template whose enabled is true |
| `template_ambiguous` | 2 | more than one enabled template of the CA has this name | give `--template` the id of the one to use; if it isn't clear which, `pkiaas template list --json` shows them, and ask the user |
| `ca_ambiguous` | 2 | more than one of the account's CAs has this name (`--ca`, `PKIAAS_CA` or `pkiaas ca set`) | give the id of the one to use instead; if it isn't clear which, `pkiaas ca list --json` shows them, and ask the user |
| `idempotency_key_reused` | 5 | the `--idempotency-key` was used for a different request in the last 24 hours | make a new key for a new request; reuse a key only to repeat exactly the same command |
| `idempotency_key_in_use` | 5 | the first request with this `--idempotency-key` hasn't finished yet | wait a minute and run the same command with the same key again; if it lasts, check on the website whether the request exists before making a new one |
| `request_not_approvable` | 5 | the request can't be approved: it has no CSR, waits for the requester to confirm their email address, or is pre-approved; or it can't be approved with changes (`--subject`, `--san`, `--not-before`, `--not-after`), since it isn't readyToBeSigned | read the message; `pkiaas request show ID --json` shows its status and hasCsr. A request without a CSR needs an approved voucher, which the user sends on the website's Pending Requests page |
| `invalid_overrides` | 1 | OpenSSL won't take the `--subject` or `--san` an approval gives, e.g. a common name longer than 64 characters; nothing was signed | fix the value the message names and approve again; the request still waits for approval |
| `request_declined` | 5 | the request was declined, which is final | nothing to approve: make a new request with `pkiaas request create` if the certificate is still needed |
| `request_issued` | 5 | the request is issued, so it can't be declined | `pkiaas request show ID --json` gives the certificate's serial; revoke it with `pkiaas cert revoke SERIAL` if it mustn't be used |
| `request_processing` | 5 | the request is being signed right now | wait a few seconds, then check it with `pkiaas request show ID --json`; one processing for more than 10 minutes (processingSince) is stuck: decline it and make a new request |
| `signing_failed` | 1 | the CA couldn't sign the request, e.g. its IoT HSM didn't answer or the template doesn't fit the CSR; the CA's log says why | tell the user, who can read the CA's log on the website; the request waits for approval again (or stays processing if the certificate was signed), so approve it again once the cause is fixed |
| `cli_outdated` | 1 | the server needs a newer pkiaas | update pkiaas with the install command in the message, then run the command again |
| `connection_failed` | 1 | the server couldn't be reached | check the server address (`--server` or `PKIAAS_SERVER`) and the network, then try again |
| `http_<status>` | 1 | the server answered with an unexpected HTTP status, e.g. http_500; the message has the request ID to quote | try again later; if it persists, report the request ID |
| `no_browser` | 1 | `pkiaas login` couldn't open a browser, and there is no terminal to wait on | ask the user to run `pkiaas login --device`, or run it and pass its address and code to the user |
| `timeout` | 1 | nobody finished the login in the browser in time | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again and approve it in the browser |
| `access_denied` | 3 | the user denied the login | ask the user whether to log in again |
| `expired_token` | 3 | the device login code expired before the user approved it | ask the user to run `pkiaas login --device` again, and to enter the code promptly |
| `invalid_state` | 3 | the browser came back from a different login | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again |
| `invalid_issuer` | 3 | the login came back from a different server | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again, with the intended `--server` |
| `invalid_request` | 3 | the server or the browser rejected the login request | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again; if it persists, update pkiaas |
| `invalid_grant` | 3 | the login code was used, expired or doesn't match | ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again |
| `invalid_client` | 3 | the server doesn't know this CLI as a client | check the server address; update pkiaas |
| `unsupported_grant_type` | 3 | the server doesn't support this login flow | update pkiaas, or log in with the other flow (`--device` or without it) |
| `temporarily_unavailable` | 3 | the server has too many pending logins | wait a minute, then ask the user to run `pkiaas login --device` again |
| `slow_down` | 3 | the server is limiting login requests from this address | wait a minute, then ask the user to run `pkiaas login` again |
